## Overview

You use command line tools every day: `git`, `mvn`, `java`, `docker`.
In this practical work, you build your own, in a group: a CLI written
with [picocli](https://picocli.info/) that reads one file, processes it,
and writes the result to another file.

**You choose what the tool does.** It can count, transform or convert
text, process an image or an audio file, encrypt or decrypt, add
metadata to pictures, and so on. Be reasonable: the point is the
processing of the data, not the algorithm.

This practical work puts [chapter 03](../chapters/03-java-intellij-maven.qmd)
(Java, IntelliJ and Maven) and
[chapter 04](../chapters/04-java-io.qmd) (Java I/O) into practice.

## Demo

Here is what such a CLI looks like from the outside. Build it:

```sh
./mvnw clean package
```

Run it without arguments, and it shows what it expects:

```text
Missing required options: '--input=<inputFile>', '--output=<outputFile>'
Usage: my-cli.jar [-hV] -i=<inputFile> [-I=<inputEncoding>] -o=<outputFile>
                  [-O=<outputEncoding>] [COMMAND]
Process an input file and write the result to an output file.
  -h, --help                  Show this help message and exit.
  -i, --input=<inputFile>     The input file.
  -I, --input-encoding=<inputEncoding>
                              The input file encoding (default: UTF-8).
  -o, --output=<outputFile>   The output file.
  -O, --output-encoding=<outputEncoding>
                              The output file encoding (default: UTF-8).
Commands:
  uppercase  Converts the input file to uppercase.
  lowercase  Converts the input file to lowercase.
```

Run one of its commands:

```sh
java -jar target/my-cli-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar \
  --input input.txt --output output.txt \
  --input-encoding UTF-8 --output-encoding US-ASCII \
  uppercase
```

```text
$ cat input.txt
Bonjour, comment ça va aujourd'hui ?

$ cat output.txt
BONJOUR, COMMENT ?A VA AUJOURD'HUI ?
```

Why is the `ç` not in the output? You know the answer since
[chapter 04](../chapters/04-java-io.qmd).

## Objectives

- Build a real CLI with subcommands, options and a help message.
- Read and write files with the Java I/O API, with the charset, the
  buffering and the error handling under your control.
- Test your processing with JUnit.
- Work as a team with Git and GitHub: issues, pull requests, reviews.
- Explain your work, in the README and in front of the class.

## Groups

You work in **groups of 3**. Pairs are allowed if the numbers do not
work out. If you have no group, come and see us and we will find you
one.

To announce your group, open a **GitHub Discussion** in the
[course organization]({{< var discussions-url >}}), category *Show and
tell*, with:

- **Title**: `[DAI {{< var year >}} Class <A or C>] PW1 - <first name> <last name>, …`
- **Description**: a few lines about what your CLI will do.

::: {.callout-important}
Do this during the first session, even if your idea is not final. We
use it to plan the presentations, and to tell you early if the scope is
too small or too large.
:::

## What your CLI must do

- Take an **input file** and an **output file** as arguments, plus
  options of your choice (for example the input and output charsets).
- Offer **at least two commands** (for example `uppercase` and
  `lowercase`), each with a help message.
- **Use the Java I/O API** from chapter 04 to read and write the files.
  You may use other libraries for the processing itself, but not to
  open, read or write the files.
- **Use what the chapter teaches**: an explicit charset, binary streams,
  or line endings, depending on your subject. We check this when we
  validate your idea.
- Be **slightly more than the course examples**, and slightly different.
  No need to shoot for the moon.
- Keep the **processing separate from the CLI**: a method that reads a
  stream and writes a stream, which the commands call. That is what you
  test (see [How to test your processing](#how-to-test-your-processing)).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Ideas, if you need one"}
Convert between encodings, normalize line endings, count words or
characters, extract or edit the metadata of pictures, convert a CSV file
to JSON, change the volume of a WAV file, turn an image to grayscale,
encrypt and decrypt a file, split and join large files.
:::

## Submission

Update the Discussion you opened at the start with:

- the link to your repository,
- the **commit hash** you want us to grade.

The deadline and the penalties are in the [Rules](#rules).

## Presentations

Each group has **8 minutes** to present its tool. Come 5 minutes before
your slot, with your computer. A video projector is available.

You are free to present as you like, but:

- show the tool **running on real files**, including a case where it
  fails.
- explain the **what** and the **why**, not every line of code.
- everyone speaks, and everyone can answer questions about the code.

## How to test your processing

Tests are new for you, so we ask for little: **separate the processing
from the CLI**, and test the processing on data built in the test. No
files on disk, no paths, nothing that depends on your machine.

Write the processing as a method that takes a `Reader` and a `Writer`
(text) or an `InputStream` and an `OutputStream` (binary). The CLI then
opens the files and calls it.

```java
public class UpperCase {
  public static void process(Reader in, Writer out) throws IOException {
    int c;
    while ((c = in.read()) != -1) {
      out.write(Character.toUpperCase(c));
    }
  }
}
```

Text: feed it a `StringReader` and collect the result in a
`StringWriter`.

```java
@Test
void upperCasesAccentedLetters() throws IOException {
  StringWriter out = new StringWriter();
  UpperCase.process(new StringReader("élève"), out);
  assertEquals("ÉLÈVE", out.toString());
}
```

Binary: use `ByteArrayInputStream` and `ByteArrayOutputStream`, and
compare with `assertArrayEquals`. When the exact output is hard to
predict (an image filter, for example), test a **property** instead: a
round trip that gives back the original, the size of the output, a
header that is preserved, or that running the tool twice changes
nothing.

```java
@Test
void encryptingTwiceGivesTheOriginalBytes() throws IOException {
  byte[] original = {0, 1, 2, (byte) 0xFF};

  ByteArrayOutputStream encrypted = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
  Xor.process(new ByteArrayInputStream(original), encrypted, 42);

  ByteArrayOutputStream decrypted = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
  Xor.process(new ByteArrayInputStream(encrypted.toByteArray()), decrypted, 42);

  assertArrayEquals(original, decrypted.toByteArray());
}
```

An **edge case** is a case that breaks a naive implementation: an empty
file, a character that does not exist in the target charset, a file
that does not end with a line ending.

## Rules

Your practical work must respect the following rules.

**The team**

- Everyone contributes to the project, and the history shows it.
- Everyone can explain the whole project in detail if we ask, not only
  the part they wrote.

**The project**

- A GitHub Discussion is opened during the **first session**, so that we
  can validate your idea.
- The files are opened, read and written with the **Java I/O API** of
  the course. No library does that part for you.
- Any Maven dependency may **process** the data once the files are open,
  an image or audio library for example. The README says which
  dependencies you use, and why.
- The application does **slightly more, and something slightly
  different**, than the examples shown in the course.
- The application **builds and runs from a fresh clone**, with
  `./mvnw clean package`, on a machine that is not yours. What we cannot
  build, we cannot grade.

**The submission**

- The Discussion is updated with the **repository link and the commit
  hash** before the deadline. We grade that commit, not what comes
  after it.
- If the repository is **private**, the teaching staff are
  collaborators. If we cannot open it at the deadline, the work counts
  as not submitted.
- Every started day of delay costs **1 point**.

**Honesty**

- State your sources: code from the internet, code generated by an AI
  tool, ideas taken elsewhere. Say what you used them for. See the
  [AI principles](../resources.qmd).
- Copying the code of another group gives a grade of **1** to everyone
  involved.

::: {.callout-caution}
These rules are not decoration. Not respecting one of them costs up to
**1 point** on the final grade, and several of them can add up.
:::

## Grades and feedback

Your grade goes into GAPS, and you receive an email with a comment for
each criterion, a general comment on your work, and the grade. If
anything is unclear, ask us.

## Tips

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="The Unix philosophy and the KISS principle"}
> Write programs that do one thing and do it well. Write programs to
> work together. Write programs to handle text streams, because that is
> a universal interface.

That is the Unix philosophy, and KISS says the same in four words:
*keep it simple, silly*. A tool that does one thing well, handles its
encodings and reports its errors, is worth more here than an ambitious
one that crashes. If your implementation is too complex, we may
penalize it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Work together on the repository"}
Add your team members as collaborators, as in
[chapter 02](../chapters/02-git-github.qmd), so everyone can push. If
your repository is private, add the teaching staff too, otherwise we
cannot grade it.

You can also protect the `main` branch, so that nobody pushes to it
directly and every change goes through a reviewed pull request. See
[GitHub's documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/managing-a-branch-protection-rule).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="How and what to present"}
Present your work as you like: slides, a live demo, a poster. But:

- no need to repeat the objectives, we know them.
- no need to walk through the code, unless a part of it is interesting,
  complex or tricky.
- focus on the **what** and the **why**.

Aim at someone who understands Java but has never heard of your project.
:::
